entries.676635e4dd5c789c85ce1b07b0403904188bf24b: <div sID="gen17922" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="33" osisID="Jer.33" sID="Jer.33"/> <div eID="gen17922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17923" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17924" type="x-p"/> The scope of this chapter is much the same with that of the foregoing chapter—to confirm the promise of the restoration of the Jews, notwithstanding the present desolations of their country and dispersions of their people. And these promises have, both in type and tendency, a reference as far forward as to the gospel church, to which this second edition of the Jewish church was at length to resign its dignities and privileges. It is here promised, I. That the city shall be rebuilt and re-established "in statu quo—in its former state," <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1-Jer.33.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. That the captives, having their sins pardoned, shall be restored, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.7-Jer.33.8">ver. 7, 8</reference>. III. That this shall redound very much to the glory of God, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">ver. 9</reference>. IV. That the country shall have both joy and plenty, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.10-Jer.33.14">ver. 10-14</reference>. V. That way shall be made for the coming of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.15-Jer.33.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. VI. That the house of David, the house of Levi, and the house of Israel, shall flourish again, and be established, and all three in the kingdom of Christ; a gospel ministry and the gospel church shall continue while the world stands, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.17-Jer.33.26">ver. 17-26</reference>.
entries.7309aa9e4304c63f8096fb0d5a65ed9ce4b56a99: <div eID="gen17924" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17923" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouraging Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17925" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Jeremiah the second time, while he was yet shut up in the court of the prison, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the maker thereof, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that formed it, to establish it; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name; <hi type="super">3</hi> Call unto me, and I will answer thee, and shew thee great and mighty things, which thou knowest not. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel, concerning the houses of this city, and concerning the houses of the kings of Judah, which are thrown down by the mounts, and by the sword; <hi type="super">5</hi> They come to fight with the Chaldeans, but <hi type="italic">it is</hi> to fill them with the dead bodies of men, whom I have slain in mine anger and in my fury, and for all whose wickedness I have hid my face from this city. <hi type="super">6</hi> Behold, I will bring it health and cure, and I will cure them, and will reveal unto them the abundance of peace and truth. <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will cause the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Israel to return, and will build them, as at the first. <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will cleanse them from all their iniquity, whereby they have sinned against me; and I will pardon all their iniquities, whereby they have sinned, and whereby they have transgressed against me. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a honour before all the nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good that I do unto them: and they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and for all the prosperity that I procure unto it. <div eID="gen17925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17926" type="x-p"/> Observe here, I. The date of this comfortable prophecy which God entrusted Jeremiah with. It is not exact in the time, only that it was after that in the foregoing chapter, when things were still growing worse and worse; it was <hi type="italic">the second time. God speaketh once, yea, twice,</hi> for the encouragement of his people. We are not only so disobedient that we have need of <hi type="italic">precept upon precept</hi> to bring us to our duty, but so distrustful that we have need of promise upon promise to bring us to our comfort. This word, as the former, <hi type="italic">came to Jeremiah</hi> when <hi type="italic">he was in prison.</hi> Note, No confinement can deprive God's people of his presence; no locks nor bars can shut out his gracious visits; nay, oftentimes <hi type="italic">as their afflictions abound their consolations much more abound,</hi> and they have the most reviving communications of his favour when the world frowns upon them. Paul's sweetest epistles were those that bore date out of a prison. <div eID="gen17926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17927" type="x-p"/> II. The prophecy itself. A great deal of comfort is wrapped up in it for the relief of the captives, to keep them from sinking into despair. Observe, <div eID="gen17927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> 1. Who it is that secures this comfort to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">v. 2</reference>): It is <hi type="italic">the Lord, the maker thereof, the Lord that framed it,</hi> He is the maker and former of heaven and earth, and therefore has all power in his hands; so it refers to Jeremiah's prayer, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.17">ch. xxxii. 17</reference>. He is the maker and former of Jerusalem, of Zion, built them at first, and therefore can rebuild them—built them for his own praise, and therefore <hi type="italic">will.</hi> He <hi type="italic">formed it, to establish it,</hi> and therefore it shall be established till those things be introduced which cannot be shaken, but shall remain for ever. He is the maker and former of this promise; he has laid the scheme for Jerusalem's restoration, and he that has formed it will establish it, he that has made the promise will make it good; for Jehovah <hi type="italic">is his name,</hi> a God giving being to his promises by the performance of them, and when he does this he is known by that name (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exod. vi. 3</reference>), a perfecting God. When the heavens and the earth were finished, then, and not till then, the creator is called <hi type="italic">Jehovah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.4">Gen. ii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17929" type="x-p"/> 2. How this comfort must be obtained and fetched in—by prayer (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Call upon me, and I will answer them.</hi> The prophet, having received some intimations of this kind, must be humbly earnest with God for further discoveries of his kind intentions. He had prayed (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.16">ch. xxxii. 16</reference>), but he must pray again. Note, Those that expect to receive comforts from God must continue instant in prayer. We must call upon him, and then he will answer us. Christ himself must <hi type="italic">ask, and it shall be given him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">I will show thee great and mighty things</hi> (give thee a clear and full prospect of them), <hi type="italic">hidden things, which,</hi> though in part discovered already, yet <hi type="italic">thou knowest not,</hi> thou canst not understand or give credit to. Or this may refer not only to the prediction of these things which Jeremiah, if he desire it, shall be favoured with, but to the performance of the things themselves which the people of God, encouraged by this prediction, must pray for. Note, Promises are given, not to supersede, but to quicken and encourage prayer. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.37">Ezek. xxxvi. 37</reference>. <div eID="gen17929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17930" type="x-p"/> 3. How deplorable the condition of Jerusalem was which made it necessary that such comforts as these should be provided for it, and notwithstanding which its restoration should be brought about in due time (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.4-Jer.33.5">v. 4, 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The houses of this city,</hi> not excepting those <hi type="italic">of the kings of Judah, are thrown down by the mounts,</hi> or engines of battery, <hi type="italic">and by the sword,</hi> or axes, or hammers. It is the same word that is used <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.9">Ezek. xxvi. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">With his axes he shall break down thy towers.</hi> The strongest stateliest houses, and those that were best furnished, were levelled with the ground. The <reference osisRef="Jer.33.5">fifth verse</reference> comes in in a parenthesis, giving a further instance of the present calamitous state of Jerusalem. Those that <hi type="italic">came to fight with the Chaldeans,</hi> to beat them off from the siege, did more hurt than good, provoked the enemy to be more fierce and furious in their assaults, so that the houses in Jerusalem were filled <hi type="italic">with the dead bodies of men,</hi> who died of the wounds they received in sallying out upon the besiegers. God says that they were such as he had <hi type="italic">slain in his anger,</hi> for the enemies' sword was his sword and their anger his anger. But, it seems, the men that were slain were generally such as had distinguished themselves by their wickedness, for they were the very men <hi type="italic">for whose wickedness</hi> God did now <hi type="italic">hide himself from this city,</hi> so that he was just in all he brought upon them. <div eID="gen17930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17931" type="x-p"/> 4. What the blessings are which God has in store for Judah and Jerusalem, such as will redress all their grievances. <div eID="gen17931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> (1.) Is their state diseased? Is it wounded? God will provide effectually for the healing of it, though the disease was thought mortal and incurable, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22">ch. vii. 22</reference>. "<hi type="italic">The whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Isa. i. 5</reference>); but (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">I will bring it health and cure;</hi> I will prevent the death, remove the sickness, and set all to rights again," <reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">ch. xxx. 17</reference>. Note, Be the case ever so desperate, if God undertake the cure, he will effect it. The sin of Jerusalem was the sickness of it (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Isa. i. 6</reference>); its reformation therefore will be its recovery. And the following words tell us how that is wrought: "<hi type="italic">I will reveal unto them the abundance of peace and truth;</hi> I will give it to them in due time, and give them an encouraging prospect of it in the mean time." <hi type="italic">Peace</hi> stands here for all good; <hi type="italic">peace and truth</hi> are peace according to the promise and in pursuance of that: or <hi type="italic">peace and truth</hi> are peace and the true religion, peace and the true worship of God, in opposition to the many falsehoods and deceits by which they had been led away from God. We may apply it more generally, and observe, [1.] That peace and truth are the great subject-matter of divine revelation. These promises here lead us to the gospel of Christ, and in that God has revealed to us <hi type="italic">peace and truth,</hi> the method of true peace—truth to direct us, peace to make us easy. <hi type="italic">Grace and truth,</hi> and abundance of both, <hi type="italic">come by Jesus Christ.</hi> Peace and truth are the life of the soul, and Christ <hi type="italic">came that we might have</hi> that <hi type="italic">life, and might have it more abundantly.</hi> Christ rules by the power of truth (<reference osisRef="John.18.37">John xviii. 37</reference>) and by it he gives <hi type="italic">abundance of peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.7">Ps. lxxii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.85.10">lxxxv. 10</reference>. [2.] That the divine revelation of peace and truth brings health and cure to all those that by faith receive it: it heals the soul of the diseases it has contracted, as it is a means of sanctification, <reference osisRef="John.17.17">John xvii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">He sent his word and healed them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Ps. cvii. 20</reference>. And it puts the soul into good order, and keeps it in a good frame and fit for the employments and enjoyments of the spiritual and divine life. <div eID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17933" type="x-p"/> (2.) Are they scattered and enslaved, and is their nation laid in ruins? "<hi type="italic">I will cause their captivity to return</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.7">v. 7</reference>), both that of Israel and that of Judah" (for though those who returned under Zerubbabel were chiefly of Judah, and Benjamin, and Levi, yet afterwards many of all the other tribes returned), "<hi type="italic">and I will rebuild them, as</hi> I built them <hi type="italic">at first.</hi>" When they by repentance do their first works God will by their restoration do his first works. <div eID="gen17933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17934" type="x-p"/> (3.) Is sin the procuring cause of all their troubles? That shall be pardoned and subdued, and so the root of the judgments shall be killed, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.8">v. 8</reference>. [1.] By sin they have become filthy, and odious to God's holiness, but God will cleanse them, and purify <hi type="italic">them from their iniquity.</hi> As those that were ceremonially unclean, and were therefore shut out from the tabernacle, when they were sprinkled with the <hi type="italic">water of purification</hi> had liberty of access to it again, so had they to their own land, and the privileges of it, when God had <hi type="italic">cleansed them from their iniquities.</hi> In allusion to that sprinkling, David prays, <hi type="italic">Purge me with hyssop.</hi> [2.] By sin they have become guilty, and obnoxious to his justice; but he will <hi type="italic">pardon all their iniquities,</hi> will remove the punishment to which for sin they were bound over. All who by sanctifying grace are cleansed from the filth of sin, by pardoning mercy are freed from the guilt of it. <div eID="gen17934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17935" type="x-p"/> (4.) Have both their sins and their sufferings turned to the dishonour of God? Their reformation and restoration shall redound as much to his praise, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">v. 9</reference>. Jerusalem thus rebuilt, Judah thus repeopled, <hi type="italic">shall be to me a name of joy,</hi> as pleasing to God as ever they have been provoking, <hi type="italic">and a praise and an honour before all the nations.</hi> They, being thus restored, shall glorify God by their obedience to him, and he shall glorify himself by his favours to them. This renewed nation shall be as much a reputation to religion as formerly it has been a reproach to it. The nations <hi type="italic">shall hear of all the good that</hi> God has wrought in them by his grace and <hi type="italic">of all the good</hi> he has wrought for them by his providence. The wonders of their return out of Babylon shall make as great a noise in the world as ever the wonders of their deliverance out of Egypt did. And <hi type="italic">they shall fear and tremble for all this goodness.</hi> [1.] The people of God themselves shall fear and tremble; they shall be much surprised at it, shall be afraid of offending so good a God and of forfeiting his favour. <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Hos. iii. 5</reference>, <hi type="italic">They shall fear the Lord and his goodness.</hi> [2.] The neighbouring nations shall fear because of the prosperity of Jerusalem, shall look upon the growing greatness of the Jewish nation as really formidable, and shall be afraid of making them their enemies. When the church is <hi type="italic">fair as the moon,</hi> and <hi type="italic">clear as the sun,</hi> she is <hi type="italic">terrible as an army with banners.</hi>
entries.3e5d80eeb6496c7af8832f9fa1e1ea5f5c7ab62e: <div eID="gen17935" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouraging Prospects. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17936" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Again there shall be heard in this place, which ye say <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> desolate without man and without beast, <hi type="italic">even</hi> in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, that are desolate, without man, and without inhabitant, and without beast, <hi type="super">11</hi> The voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the voice of them that shall say, Praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> good; for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever: <hi type="italic">and</hi> of them that shall bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . For I will cause to return the captivity of the land, as at the first, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; Again in this place, which is desolate without man and without beast, and in all the cities thereof, shall be a habitation of shepherds causing <hi type="italic">their</hi> flocks to lie down. <hi type="super">13</hi> In the cities of the mountains, in the cities of the vale, and in the cities of the south, and in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, shall the flocks pass again under the hands of him that telleth <hi type="italic">them,</hi> saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> Behold, the days come, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that I will perform that good thing which I have promised unto the house of Israel and to the house of Judah. <hi type="super">15</hi> In those days, and at that time, will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land. <hi type="super">16</hi> In those days shall Judah be saved, and Jerusalem shall dwell safely: and this <hi type="italic">is the name</hi> wherewith she shall be called, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our righteousness. <div eID="gen17936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17937" type="x-p"/> Here is a further prediction of the happy state of Judah and Jerusalem after their glorious return out of captivity, issuing gloriously at length in the kingdom of the Messiah. <div eID="gen17937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17938" type="x-p"/> I. It is promised that the people who were long in sorrow shall again be filled with joy. Every one concluded now that the country would lie for ever desolate, that <hi type="italic">no beasts</hi> would be found in the land of Judah, no inhabitant <hi type="italic">in the streets of Jerusalem,</hi> and consequently there would be nothing but universal and perpetual melancholy (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.10">v. 10</reference>); but, though weeping may endure for a time, joy will return. It was threatened (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">ch. vii. 34</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">xvi. 9</reference>) that <hi type="italic">the voice of joy and gladness should cease</hi> there; but here it is promised that they shall revive again, that <hi type="italic">the voice of joy and gladness shall be heard</hi> there, because <hi type="italic">the captivity shall be returned;</hi> for then was <hi type="italic">their mouth filled with laughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.126.1-Ps.126.2">Ps. cxxvi. 1, 2</reference>. 1. There shall be common joy there, <hi type="italic">the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride;</hi> marriages shall again be celebrated, as formerly, with songs, which in Babylon they had laid aside, for their harps were hung on the willow-trees. 2. There shall be religious joy there; temple-songs shall be revived, <hi type="italic">the Lord's songs,</hi> which they could not <hi type="italic">sing in a strange land.</hi> There shall be heard in their private houses, and in the cities of Judah, as well as in the temple, <hi type="italic">the voice of those that shall say, Praise the Lord of hosts.</hi> Note, Nothing is more the praise and honour of a people than to have God the glory of it, the glory both of the power and of the goodness by which it is effected; they shall praise him both as <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts</hi> and as the God who <hi type="italic">is good</hi> and whose <hi type="italic">mercy endures for ever.</hi> This, though a song of old, yet, being sung upon this fresh occasion, will be a new song. We find this literally fulfilled at their return out of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">Ezra iii. 11</reference>. They sang together in praising the Lord, <hi type="italic">because he is good, for his mercy endures for ever.</hi> The public worship of God shall be diligently and constantly attended upon: <hi type="italic">They shall bring the sacrifice of praise to the house of the Lord.</hi> All the sacrifices were intended for the praise of God, but this seems to be meant of the spiritual sacrifices of humble adorations and joyful thanksgivings, <hi type="italic">the calves of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Hos. xiv. 2</reference>), which <hi type="italic">shall please the Lord better than an ox of bullock.</hi> The Jews say that in the days of the Messiah all sacrifices shall cease but <hi type="italic">the sacrifice of praise,</hi> and to those days this promise has a further reference. <div eID="gen17938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17939" type="x-p"/> II. It is promised that the country, which had lain long depopulated, shall be replenished and stocked again. It was now desolate, <hi type="italic">without man and without beast;</hi> but, after their return, the pastures shall again be <hi type="italic">clothed with flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.13">Ps. lxv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">In all the cities of Judah and Benjamin there shall be a habitation of shepherds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.33.12-Jer.33.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. This intimates, 1. The wealth of the country, after their return. It shall not be a habitation of beggars, who have nothing, but of shepherds and husbandmen, men of substance, with good stocks upon the ground they have returned to. 2. The peace of the country. It shall not be a habitation of soldiers, not shall there be tents and barracks set up to lodge them, but there shall be shepherds; tents; for they shall hear no more the alarms of war, nor shall there be any to make even the shepherds afraid. See <reference osisRef="Ps.144.13-Ps.144.14">Ps. cxliv. 13, 14</reference>. 3. The industry of the country, and their return to their original plainness and simplicity, from which, in the corrupt ages, they had sadly degenerated. The seed of Jacob, in their beginning, gloried in this, that they were shepherds (<reference osisRef="Gen.47.3">Gen. xlvii. 3</reference>), and so they shall now be again, giving themselves wholly to that innocent employment, <hi type="italic">causing their flocks to lie down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.12">v. 12</reference>) and to <hi type="italic">pass under the hands of him that telleth them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.13">v. 13</reference>); for, though their flocks are numerous, they are not numberless, nor shall they omit to number them, that they may know if any be missing and may seek after it. Note, It is the prudence of those who have ever so much of the world to keep an account of what they have. Some think that they <hi type="italic">pass under the hand of him that telleth them</hi> that they may be tithed, <reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">Lev. xxvii. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we may take the comfort of what we have when God has had his dues out of it. Now because it seemed incredible that a people, reduced as now they were, should ever recover such a degree of peace and plenty as this, here is subjoined a general ratification of these promises (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will perform that good thing which I have promised.</hi> Though the promise may sometimes work slowly towards an accomplishment, it works surely. <hi type="italic">The days will come,</hi> though they are long in coming. <div eID="gen17939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> III. To crown all these blessings which God has in store for them, here is a promise of the Messiah, and of that everlasting righteousness which he should bring in (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.15-Jer.33.16">v. 15, 16</reference>), and probably this is <hi type="italic">that good thing,</hi> that great good thing, which in the latter days, days that were yet to come, God would perform, as he had promised to Judah and Israel, and to which their return out of captivity and their settlement again in their own land was preparatory. <hi type="italic">From the captivity to Christ</hi> is one of the famous periods, <reference osisRef="Matt.1.17">Matt. i. 17</reference>. This promise of the Messiah we had before (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">ch. xxiii. 5, 6</reference>), and there it came in as a confirmation of the promise of the shepherds whom God would set over them, which would make one think that the promise here concerning the shepherds and their flocks, which introduces it, is to be understood figuratively. Christ is here prophesied of, 1. As a rightful King. He is a <hi type="italic">branch of righteousness,</hi> not a usurper, for he <hi type="italic">grows up unto David,</hi> descends from his loins, with whom the covenant of royalty was made, and is that seed with whom that covenant should be established, so that his title is unexceptionable. 2. As a righteous king, righteous in enacting laws, waging wars, and giving judgment, righteous in vindicating those that suffer wrong and punishing those that do wrong: <hi type="italic">He shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.</hi> This may point at Zerubbabel, in the type, who governed with equity, not as Jehoiakim had done (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.17">ch. xxii. 17</reference>); but it has a further reference to him to whom all judgment is committed and who shall <hi type="italic">judge the world in righteousness.</hi> 3. As a king that shall protect his subjects from all injury. By him <hi type="italic">Judah shall be saved</hi> from wrath and the curse, and, being so saved, <hi type="italic">Jerusalem shall dwell safely,</hi> quiet from the fear of evil, and enjoying a holy security and serenity of mind, in a dependence upon the conduct of this prince of peace, this prince of their peace. 4. As a king that shall be praised by his subjects: "<hi type="italic">This is the name whereby they shall call him</hi>" (so the Chaldee reads it, the Syriac, and vulgar Latin); "this name of his they shall celebrate and triumph in, and by this name they shall call upon him." It may be read, more agreeably to the original, <hi type="italic">This is he who shall call her, The Lord our righteousness.</hi> As Moses's altar is called <hi type="italic">Jehovah-nissi</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.15">Exod. xvii. 15</reference>), and Jerusalem <hi type="italic">Jehovah-shammah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.48.35">Ezek. xlviii. 35</reference>), intimating that they glory in Jehovah as present with them and <hi type="italic">their banner,</hi> so here the city is called <hi type="italic">The Lord our righteousness,</hi> because they glory in Jehovah as their righteousness. That which was before said to be the name of Christ (says Mr. Gataker) is here made the name of Jerusalem, the city of the Messiah, the church of Christ. He it is that imparts righteousness to her, for he is <hi type="italic">made of God to us righteousness,</hi> and she, by bearing that name, professes to have her whole righteousness, not from herself, but from him. <hi type="italic">In the Lord have I righteousness and strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa. xlv. 24</reference>. And <hi type="italic">we are made the righteousness of God in him.</hi> The inhabitants of Jerusalem shall have this name of the Messiah so much in their mouths that they shall themselves be called by it.
entries.d9101a03f2517787e966a3e45277c5885a00b0bc: <div eID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Security of God's Covenants; The Covenant of Priesthood. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17941" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel; <hi type="super">18</hi> Neither shall the priests the Levites want a man before me to offer burnt offerings, and to kindle meat offerings, and to do sacrifice continually. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">20</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; If ye can break my covenant of the day, and my covenant of the night, and that there should not be day and night in their season; <hi type="super">21</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> may also my covenant be broken with David my servant, that he should not have a son to reign upon his throne; and with the Levites the priests, my ministers. <hi type="super">22</hi> As the host of heaven cannot be numbered, neither the sand of the sea measured: so will I multiply the seed of David my servant, and the Levites that minister unto me. <hi type="super">23</hi> Moreover the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">24</hi> Considerest thou not what this people have spoken, saying, The two families which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath chosen, he hath even cast them off? thus they have despised my people, that they should be no more a nation before them. <hi type="super">25</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; If my covenant <hi type="italic">be</hi> not with day and night, <hi type="italic">and if</hi> I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth; <hi type="super">26</hi> Then will I cast away the seed of Jacob, and David my servant, <hi type="italic">so</hi> that I will not take <hi type="italic">any</hi> of his seed <hi type="italic">to be</hi> rulers over the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: for I will cause their captivity to return, and have mercy on them. <div eID="gen17941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17942" type="x-p"/> Three of God's covenants, that of royalty with David and his seed, that of the priesthood with Aaron and his seed, and that of Peculiarity with Abraham and his seed, seemed to be all broken and lost while the captivity lasted; but it is here promised that, notwithstanding that interruption and discontinuance for a time, they shall all three take place again, and the true intents and meaning of them all shall be abundantly answered in the New Testament blessings, typified by those conferred on the Jews after their return out of captivity. <div eID="gen17942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17943" type="x-p"/> I. The covenant of royalty shall be secured and the promises of it shall have their full accomplishment in the kingdom of Christ, the Son of David, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.17">v. 17</reference>. The throne of Israel was overturned in the captivity; the crown had fallen from their head; there was not <hi type="italic">a man to sit on the throne of Israel;</hi> Jeconiah was written childless. After their return the house of David made a figure again; but it in the Messiah that this promise is performed that <hi type="italic">David shall never want a man to sit on the throne of Israel,</hi> and that David shall have <hi type="italic">always a son to reign upon his throne.</hi> For as long as the man Christ Jesus sits on the right hand of the throne of God, rules the world, and rules it for the good of the church, to which he is a quickening head, and glorified head over all things, as long as he is <hi type="italic">King upon the holy hill of Zion,</hi> David does not want a successor, nor is the covenant with him broken. When the first-begotten was brought into the world it was declared concerning him, <hi type="italic">The Lord God shall give him the throne of his father David and he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.32-Luke.1.33">Luke i. 32, 33</reference>. For the confirmation of this it is promised, 1. That the covenant with David shall be as firm as the ordinances of heaven, to the stability of which that of God's promise is compared, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35">ch. xxxi. 35, 36</reference>. There is a covenant of nature, by which the common course of providence is settled and on which it is founded, here called <hi type="italic">a covenant of the day and the night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.25">25</reference>), because this is one of the articles of it, That there shall be <hi type="italic">day and night in their season,</hi> according to the distinction put between them in the creation, when God divided between the light and the darkness, and established their mutual succession, and a government to each, that <hi type="italic">the sun</hi> should <hi type="italic">rule by day</hi> and <hi type="italic">the moon and stars by night</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.4-Gen.1.5">Gen. i. 4, 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.16">16</reference>), which establishment was renewed after the flood (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Gen. viii. 22</reference>), and has continued ever since, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.2">Ps. xix. 2</reference>. The <hi type="italic">morning and</hi> the <hi type="italic">evening</hi> have both of them their regular <hi type="italic">outgoings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.65.8">Ps. lxv. 8</reference>); the <hi type="italic">day-spring knows its place, knows its time,</hi> and keeps both, so do <hi type="italic">the shadows of the evening;</hi> and, while the world stands, this course shall not be altered, this covenant shall not be broken. <hi type="italic">The ordinances of heaven and earth</hi> (of this communication between heaven and earth, the dominion of these ordinances of heaven upon the earth), <hi type="italic">which</hi> God has <hi type="italic">appointed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.25">v. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.33">compare Job xxxviii. 33</reference>), shall never be disappointed. Thus firm shall the covenant of redemption be with the Redeemer—God's servant, but David our King, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.21">v. 21</reference>. This intimates that Christ shall have a church on earth to the world's end; he shall see a seed in which he shall prolong his days till time and day shall be no more. Christ's <hi type="italic">kingdom is an everlasting kingdom;</hi> and when <hi type="italic">the end cometh,</hi> and not till then, it <hi type="italic">shall be delivered up to God,</hi> even <hi type="italic">the Father.</hi> But it intimates that the condition of it in this world shall be intermixed and counterchanged, prosperity and adversity succeeding each other, as light and darkness, day and night. But this is plainly taught us, that, as sure as we may be that, though the sun will set tonight, it will rise again tomorrow morning, whether we live to see it or no, so sure we may be that, though the kingdom of the Redeemer in the world may for a time be clouded and eclipsed by corruptions and persecutions, yet it will shine forth again, and recover its lustre, in the time appointed. 2. That <hi type="italic">the seed of David</hi> shall be as numerous <hi type="italic">as the host of heaven,</hi> that is, the spiritual seed of the Messiah, that shall be born to him by the efficacy of his gospel and his Spirit working with it. <hi type="italic">From the womb of the morning he shall have the dew of their youth,</hi> to be his <hi type="italic">willing people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. Christ's seed are not, as David's were, his successors, but his subjects; yet the day is coming when they also shall reign with him (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">As the host of heaven cannot be numbered, so will I multiply the seed of David,</hi> so that there shall be no danger of the kingdom's being extinct, or extirpated, for want of heirs. The children are numerous; <hi type="italic">and, if children, then heirs.</hi> <div eID="gen17943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17944" type="x-p"/> II. The covenant of priesthood shall be secured, and the promises of that also shall have their full accomplishment. This seemed likewise to be forgotten during the captivity, when there was no altar, no temple service, for the priests to attend upon; but this also shall revive. It did so; immediately upon their coming back to Jerusalem there were priests and Levites ready <hi type="italic">to offer burnt-offerings</hi> and to <hi type="italic">do sacrifice continually</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.2-Ezra.3.3">Ezra iii. 2, 3</reference>), as is here promised, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.18">v. 18</reference>. But that priesthood soon grew corrupt; <hi type="italic">the covenant of Levi</hi> was <hi type="italic">profaned</hi> (as appears <reference osisRef="Mal.2.8">Mal. ii. 8</reference>), and in the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans it came to a final period. We must therefore look elsewhere for the performance of this word, that the covenant with the Levites, the priests, God's ministers, shall be as firm, and last as long, as the covenant <hi type="italic">with the day and the night.</hi> And we find it abundantly performed, 1. In the priesthood of Christ, which supersedes that of Aaron, and is the substance of that shadow. While that great <hi type="italic">high priest of our profession</hi> is always appearing <hi type="italic">in the presence of God for us,</hi> presenting the virtue of his blood by which he made atonement in the incense of his intercession, it may truly be said that <hi type="italic">the Levites do not want a man before God to offer continually,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.7.3">Heb. vii. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.17">17</reference>. He is a priest for ever. The covenant of the priesthood is called <hi type="italic">a covenant of peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.25.12">Num. xxv. 12</reference>), of <hi type="italic">life and peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.2.5">Mal. ii. 5</reference>. Now we are sure that this covenant is not broken, nor in the least weakened, while Jesus Christ is himself our life and our peace. This covenant of priesthood is here again and again joined with that of royalty, for Christ is a <hi type="italic">priest upon his throne,</hi> as Melchizedek. 2. In a settled gospel ministry. While there are faithful ministers to preside in religious assemblies, and to offer up the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise, <hi type="italic">the priests, the Levites,</hi> do not want successors, and such as <hi type="italic">have obtained a more excellent ministry.</hi> The apostle makes those that preach the gospel to come in the room of those that served at the altar, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.13-1Cor.9.14">1 Cor. ix. 13, 14</reference>. 3. In all true believers, who are <hi type="italic">a holy priesthood, a royal priesthood</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Peter ii. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">9</reference>), who are <hi type="italic">made to our God kings and priests</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev. i. 6</reference>); they <hi type="italic">offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God,</hi> and themselves, in the first place, <hi type="italic">living sacrifices.</hi> Of these Levites this promise must be understood (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.22">v. 22</reference>), that they shall be as numerous <hi type="italic">as the sand of the sea,</hi> the same that is promised concerning Israel in general (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 17</reference>); for all God's spiritual Israel are spiritual priests, <reference osisRef="Rev.5.9-Rev.5.10">Rev. v. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9 Rev.7.15">vii. 9, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen17944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17945" type="x-p"/> III. The covenant of peculiarity likewise shall be secured and the promises of that covenant shall have their full accomplishment in the gospel Israel. Observe, 1. How this covenant was looked upon as broken during the captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.24">v. 24</reference>. God asks the prophet, "Hast though not heard, and dost <hi type="italic">thou not consider, what this people have spoken?</hi>" either the enemies of Israel, who triumphed in the extirpation of a people that had made such a noise in the world, or the unbelieving Israelites themselves, "<hi type="italic">this people</hi> among whom thou dwellest;" they have broken covenant with God, and then quarrel with him as if he had not dealt faithfully with them. <hi type="italic">The two families which the Lord hath chosen,</hi> Israel and Judah, whereas they were but one when he chose them, <hi type="italic">he hath even cast them off. "Thus have they despised my people,</hi> that is, despised the privilege of being my people as if it were a privilege of no value at all." The neighbouring nations despised them as now <hi type="italic">no more a nation,</hi> but the ruins of a nation, and looked upon all their honour as laid in the dust; but, 2. See how firm the covenant stands notwithstanding, as firm as that with day and night; sooner will God suffer day and night to cease then he will <hi type="italic">cast away the seed of Jacob.</hi> This cannot refer to the seed of Jacob according to the flesh, for they are cast away, but to the Christian church, in which all these promises were to be lodged, as appears by the apostle's discourse, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>, &c. Christ is that seed of David that is to be perpetual dictator to the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and, as this people shall never want such a king, so this king shall never want such a people. Christianity shall continue in the dominion of Christ, and the subjection of Christians to him, till day and night come to an end. And, as a pledge of this, that promise is again repeated, <hi type="italic">I will cause their captivity to return;</hi> and, having brought them back, <hi type="italic">I will have mercy on them.</hi> To whom this promise refers appears <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Gal. vi. 16</reference>, where all that <hi type="italic">walk according to the gospel rule</hi> are made to be the <hi type="italic">Israel of God,</hi> on whom <hi type="italic">peace and mercy</hi> shall be.  <chapter eID="Jer.33"/> <div eID="gen17945" type="x-p"/>

entries.ac9de3b552dc9c37a93da6dc1ed9ccc6a9a8377e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10331"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 33</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.33.1-Jer.33.26">Jr 33:1-26</reference>. Prophecy of the Restoration from Babylon, and of Messiah as King and Priest.</title> <div sID="gen18437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10331"/><hi type="bold">1. shut up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.32.2">Jr 32:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2Ti 2:9</reference>). Though Jeremiah was shut up in bondage, the word of God was "not bound." <div eID="gen18437" type="x-p"/>
entries.30faf09d5754f19bb3a67e9962ff50220ce3f301: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10332"/><div sID="gen18438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10332"/><hi type="bold">2. maker thereof--</hi>rather, "the doer of it," namely, that which Jeremiah is about to prophesy, the restoration of Israel, an act which is thought now impossible, but which the Almighty will effect.<div eID="gen18438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">formed it--</hi>namely, Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jr 32:44</reference>) [Calvin]. Rather, "that formed," that is, moulds His purpose into due shape for execution (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Is 37:26</reference>).<div eID="gen18439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18440" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord ... his name--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Ex 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen18440" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6d12c85e322fbe25a79feae2f2b776b86e57304: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10333"/><div sID="gen18441" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10333"/><hi type="bold">3. Call ... I will answer--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.29.12">Jr 29:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.15">Psa 91:15</reference>). Jeremiah, as the representative of the people of God, is urged by God to pray for that which God has determined to grant; namely, the restoration. God's promises are not to slacken, but to quicken the prayers of His people (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.13">Psa 132:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">7</reference>).<div eID="gen18441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18442" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty things--</hi>Hebrew, "inaccessible things," that is, incredible, hard to man's understanding [Maurer], namely, the restoration of the Jews, an event despaired of. "Hidden," or "recondite" [Piscator].<div eID="gen18442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18443" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou knowest not--</hi>Yet God had revealed those things to Jeremiah, but the unbelief of the people in rejecting the grace of God had caused him to forget God's promise, as though the case of the people admitted of no remedy. <div eID="gen18443" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5fd761999380a9fcaa66797484c73e7f4efb291: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10334"/><div sID="gen18444" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10334"/><hi type="bold">4. houses ... thrown down by the mounts--</hi>namely, by the missiles cast from the besiegers' mounds (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.24">Jr 32:24</reference>); "and by the sword" follows properly, as, after missiles had prepared the way, the foe next advanced to close quarters "with the sword." <div eID="gen18444" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1cbc9ba928021cedec79adc89b2b212e39c2cc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10335"/><div sID="gen18445" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10335"/><hi type="bold">5. They--</hi>the Jews; the defenders of the "houses" (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.4">Jr 33:4</reference>), "come forward to fight with the Chaldeans," who burst into the city through the "thrown-down houses," but all the effect that they produce "is, to fill them (the houses) with" their own "dead bodies." <div eID="gen18445" type="x-p"/>
entries.f65e02d1c51dbf0b9466b83bbce77613a51ed736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10336"/><div sID="gen18446" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10336"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Jer.30.17">Jr 30:17</reference>). The answer to Jeremiah's mournful question (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>).<div eID="gen18446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18447" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cure--</hi>literally, the long linen bandage employed in dressing wounds.<div eID="gen18447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18448" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth--</hi>that is, stability; I will bring forth for them abundant and permanent peace, that is, prosperity. <div eID="gen18448" type="x-p"/>
entries.9c8665c968e7931ade7aadd7f1335f9bff2b324d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10337"/><div sID="gen18449" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10337"/><hi type="bold">7. cause ... to return--</hi>that is, reverse (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.11">Jr 33:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.44">Jr 32:44</reference>). The specification, both of "Judah" and "Israel," can only apply fully to the future restoration.<div eID="gen18449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18450" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as at the first--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">Is 1:26</reference>). <div eID="gen18450" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd64128806cb5a84baaf83df2b10ac2c6f858a1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10338"/><div sID="gen18451" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10338"/><hi type="bold">8. cleanse--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.36.25">Eze 36:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.13">He 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.14">14</reference>). Alluding to the legal rites of purification.<div eID="gen18451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18452" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all their iniquity ... all their iniquities--</hi>both the principle of sin within, and its outward manifestations in acts. The repetition is in order that the Jews may consider how great is the grace of God in not merely pardoning (as to the punishment), but also cleansing them (as to the pollution of guilt); not merely one iniquity, but all (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.18">Mi 7:18</reference>). <div eID="gen18452" type="x-p"/>
entries.508539b358f5f82fcbe2c14c043e91f63035e69d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10339"/><div sID="gen18453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10339"/><hi type="bold">9. it--</hi>the city.<div eID="gen18453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18454" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a name ... a praise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jr 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.7">Is 62:7</reference>).<div eID="gen18454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18455" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them--</hi>the inhabitants of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen18455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall fear ... for all the goodness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>). The Gentiles shall be led to "fear" God by the proofs of His power displayed in behalf of the Jews; the ungodly among them shall "tremble" for fear of God's judgments on them; the penitent shall reverentially fear and be converted to Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.15">Psa 102:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.3">Is 60:3</reference>). <div eID="gen18456" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">Jr 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.16.9">16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18459" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Praise the Lord, &c.--</hi>the words of <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1">Psa 136:1</reference>, which were actually used by the Jews at their restoration (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">Ezr 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen18459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18460" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sacrifice of praise--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.107.22">Psa 107:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">116:17</reference>). entries.c9795d68c688e2928108c20413c70c5509a32968: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10342"/><div sID="gen18461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10342"/><hi type="bold">12. habitation of shepherds ... flocks--</hi>in contrast to <reference osisRef="Jer.33.10">Jr 33:10</reference>, "without man ... inhabitant ... without beast" (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.43">Jr 32:43</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.24">Jr 31:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.19">50:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">Is 65:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18461" type="x-p"/>
entries.86053e0e89fd753d90f5513c894d6210d66dfdff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10343"/><div sID="gen18462" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10343"/><hi type="bold">13. pass ... under ... hands of him that telleth them--</hi>Shepherds, in sending forth and bringing back their sheep to the folds, count them by striking each as it passes with a rod, implying the shepherd's provident care that not one should be lost (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.32">Le 27:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.14">Mi 7:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.12">17:12</reference>). <div eID="gen18462" type="x-p"/>
entries.983c35e38cc7e1e726264020224af519918da76a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10344"/><div sID="gen18463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10344"/><hi type="bold">14. perform--</hi>"I will make to rise"; God's promise having for a time seemed to "lie" dead and abortive [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18463" type="x-p"/>

Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jr 23:5</reference>.<div eID="gen18464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the land--</hi>the Holy Land: Israel and Judah (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>). <div eID="gen18465" type="x-p"/>
entries.469c34999f6a28ce0e01c31f78922b7d1e9f9086: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10346"/><div sID="gen18466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10346"/><hi type="bold">16. Jerusalem--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>, instead of this, it is "Israel." "The name" in the Hebrew has here to be supplied from that passage; and for "he" (Messiah, the antitypical "Israel"), the antecedent there (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">Is 49:3</reference>), we have "she" here, that is, Jerusalem. She is called by the same name as Messiah, "The Lord Our Righteousness," by virtue of the mystical oneness between her (as the literal representative of the spiritual Church) and her Lord and Husband. Thus, whatever belongs to the Head belongs also to the members (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.30">Ep 5:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">32</reference>). Hence, the Church is called "Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">1Co 12:12</reference>). The Church hereby professes to draw all her righteousness from Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Is 45:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.25">25</reference>). It is for the sake of Jerusalem, literal and spiritual, that God the Father gives this name (Jehovah, Tsidkenu, "The Lord our Righteousness") to Christ. <div eID="gen18466" type="x-p"/>

entries.37f306963a1752928bc9530f57a145c5917435fe: <div eID="gen30231" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30232" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30233" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30233" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30232" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30234" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophet predicts a restoration of Israel and Judah to the favor of God, attended with such glorious circumstances as shall astonish all the world, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1-Jer.33.9">Jer 33:1-9</reference>. Their prosperity from that period is then described by a beautiful enumeration of circumstances, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.10-Jer.33.13">Jer 33:10-13</reference>. Thus leads to the promise of the Messiah, the grand subject of the prophetical writings, and the happiness and stability which the children of Israel shall enjoy under his government; promises which, in so far as they respect the great body of the Jews, remain still to be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.14-Jer.33.26">Jer 33:14-26</reference>. <div eID="gen30234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30235" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30236" type="x-p"/> Moreover the word of the Lord - This was in the eleventh year of the reign of Zedekiah, Jeremiah being still shut up in prison: but he was now in the court of the prison, where the elders and the king's officers, etc., might consult him with the greater ease; for they continued to inquire, foolishly thinking, that if he would but prophesy good things, that these must come, or that he had sufficient power with God to induce him to alter his mind, - destroy the Chaldeans, and deliver the city.
entries.b1ba4ce4c0a85d2579e5e6052568887bf321acd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30237" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord the Maker thereof - עשה osah, the doer of it. That is, he who is to perform that which he is now about to promise. <div eID="gen30237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30238" type="x-p"/> Thus translated by Dahler. - <div eID="gen30238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30239" type="x-p"/> Voici ce que dit l'Eternel, qui fait ce qu'il a dit. - "Thus saith the Lord, who doth that which he hath said." <div eID="gen30239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30240" type="x-p"/> The word Jehovah, not Lord, should be used in all such places as this.
entries.2134f1d76ce9db12691a9184302d0a4700245bb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30241" type="x-p"/> Call unto eve, and I will answer thee - To me alone it belongs to reveal what is future; and the stupendous things which are now coming are known only to myself. These idolaters go to their gods to get information relative to the issue of the present commotions; but there is no light in them. Ask thou, O Jeremiah, and I will tell thee the great and mighty things which even thou knowest not.
entries.1060afbdb371265fa9fa82239ed73dcca7e59f97: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30242" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord - This is a new confirmation of what has already been said, viz., The city shall fall, a number of the inhabitants shall perish, the rest shall be carried into captivity; but the nation shall be preserved, and the people return from their captivity.
entries.c77190753ecfbada305e91c78902abaa06e45014: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30243" type="x-p"/> Behold I will bring it health and, cure - ארכה aruchah, an extensive plaister; or, as we phrase it, a plaister as large as the sore. I will repair the losses of families by numerous births, and bless the land with fertility.
entries.5d616a99403780ed017099b080a662d01172111d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30244" type="x-p"/> The captivity of Judah and the captivity of Israel - This must respect the latter times, for the ten tribes did not return with the Jews at the termination of the seventy years.
entries.371b726b1fa5438870b7e6a87cc11deb12c7a2cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30245" type="x-p"/> I will cleanse them - These promises of pardon and holiness must be referred to their state under the Gospel, when they shall have received Jesus as the promised Messiah.
entries.083a2b49a8f298d248a510c3c5a021cce9d6270b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30246" type="x-p"/> They shall fear and tremble - The surrounding nations shall be persuaded that it is the hand of the Almighty that has wrought this change in your behalf; and shall fear to molest you, and tremble lest they should incur the displeasure of your God by doing you any kind of evil.
entries.000d686facf180eea9350d6cf78c53b16f288673: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30247" type="x-p"/> The voice of them that shall say, Praise the Lord of hosts - That is, the voice of the Levites in the sacred service: intimating that the temple should be rebuilt, and the public service restored.
entries.56f6651aec67c7a2ba8431fe5c373c04f48305ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30248" type="x-p"/> A habitation of shepherds - See on <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer 31:12</reference> (note).
entries.f87ebf068b21c0cc287872b3002eafdde9e1ad14: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen30248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30249" type="x-p"/> Behold the days come - See <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">Jer 23:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.31.31">Jer 31:31</reference>. <div eID="gen30249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30250" type="x-p"/> That good thing which I have promised - By my prophets: for those who have predicted the captivity have also foretold its conclusion, though not in such express terms as Jeremiah did. See <reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Hos 1:10</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Hos 2:15</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.11">Hos 6:11</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Amo.9.14">Amo 9:14</reference>, etc., and <reference osisRef="Jer.3.12">Jer 3:12</reference>, etc. The end of the captivity has been foretold by Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mic 7:9</reference>, etc.; Zephaniah, <reference osisRef="Zep.3.10">Zep 3:10</reference>, etc.; and by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jer 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jer 23:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">Jer 29:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jer 32:37</reference>. The Targum explains <reference osisRef="Jer.32.14">Jer 32:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.15">Jer 32:15</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.32.16">Jer 32:16</reference> of the Messiah.
entries.21770a8e44baecc2bb0347507a949d3b930c466e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30251" type="x-p"/> And this is the name wherewith she shall be called, The Lord our Righteousness - See what has been said on <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference> (note), which is generally supposed to be a strictly parallel passage: but they are very different, and I doubt whether they mean exactly the same thing. As to our translation here, it is ignorant, and almost impious; it says that Jerusalem, for that is the antecedent, shall be called The Lord our Righteousness. The pronoun לה lah, which is translated her, is the masculine affix, in the Chaldaic form, which frequently occurs; and Dr. Blayney translates, "And this is He whom Jehovah shall call our righteousness," or Justification. Perhaps there is a sense which these words will bear far more congenial to the scope of the place. I will give the original, as before: וזה אשר יקרא לה יהוה צדקנו vezeh asher yikra lah, Yehovah tsidkenu, "And this one who shall call to her is the Lord our Justification;" that is, the salvation of the Jews shall take place when Jesus Christ is proclaimed to them as their Justifier, and they receive him as such. <div eID="gen30251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30252" type="x-p"/> Instead of לה lah, her or him, Chaldaice, the Vulgate, Chaldee, and Syriac have read לו lo, him, less ambiguously; and this reading is supported by one or two MSS. This emendation renders the passage here more conformable to that in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jer 23:6</reference>; but if the translation above be admitted, all embarrassment is gone. <div eID="gen30252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30253" type="x-p"/> One of my own MSS. has לה loh, with the masculine points, and no mappik on the ה he; and for tsidkenu has צדקינו tsidkeynu, the contracted plural form, our righteousness: but this may be a mistake. The passages in this and the twenty-third chapter were not, I am satisfied, intended to express the same thing. I suppose that above refers to the preaching or proclaiming Christ crucified to the Jews, when the time shall arrive in which they shall be incorporated with the Gentile Church. Dahler translates this as he did that in chap. 23, which is a perfect oversight: but paraphrastic renderings are too often introduced by this learned foreigner.
entries.9feb5fde84cf990ed461536395706161db7e561c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30254" type="x-p"/> Neither shall the priests the Levites want a man - This is a repetition of the promise made to Phinehas, <reference osisRef="Num.25.13">Num 25:13</reference>.
entries.e6964409fa85bfc744a4c38b027f50909a078977: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30255" type="x-p"/> If ye can break my covenant of the day - See the note on <reference osisRef="Jer.31.36">Jer 31:36</reference>.
entries.a7d6cc7df04ad694a408b7759be48f1c819d363e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30256" type="x-p"/> So will I multiply the seed of David - This must be understood of the spiritual David, Jesus Christ, and his progeny, genuine Christians. The two families which God chose for the priesthood, that of Aaron and Phinehas, or, on its being taken away from him, that of Ithamar, <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.35">1Sam 2:35</reference>, are both extinct. Nor has the office of high priest, or priest of any kind offering sacrifice, been exercised among the Jews for nearly eighteen hundred years; therefore what is said here of the priesthood must refer to the spiritual priesthood, at the head of which is Jesus Christ.
entries.40ea91195a16015651277fe9175e7dfb841bbf8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30257" type="x-p"/> The two families which the Lord hath chosen - Some think these refer to the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah; but they never can be considered as two distinct families, being of one and the same race. Others think that the families of Jacob and David are intended; but neither were these distinct. If the two families which had the priesthood be not meant, then the regal family of David, and the sacerdotal family of Jacob through Levi, may be designed. See <reference osisRef="Jer.33.26">Jer 33:26</reference>. Following the spiritual interpretation, neither the regal nor sacerdotal family has failed; for Jesus is a King and a Priest, and all true believers in him are kings and priests unto God and the Lamb. And the highest King that ever reigned is He who is the seed of David, King of kings and Lord of lords, who has all power in heaven and in earth.  <chapter eID="Jer.33"/> <div eID="gen30257" type="x-p"/>

entries.03d9d60fe6481a72eeb19475de6940a767562601: <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1">Jer 33:1</reference> <div eID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> While Jeremiah was still in confinement in the court of the prison belonging to the palace (see <reference osisRef="Jer.32.2">Jer 32:2</reference>), the word of the Lord came to him the second time. This word of God is attached by שׁנית to the promise of Jer 32. It followed, too, not long, perhaps, after the other, which it further serves to confirm. - After the command to call on Him, that He might make known to him great and hidden things (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference>), the Lord announces that, although Jerusalem shall be destroyed by the Chaldeans, He shall yet restore it, bring back the captives of Judah and Israel, purify the city from its iniquities, and make it the glory and praise of all the people of the earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.4-Jer.33.9">Jer 33:4-9</reference>), so that in it and in the whole land joy will again prevail (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.10-Jer.33.13">Jer 33:10-13</reference>). Then the Lord promises the restoration of the kingdom through the righteous sprout of David - of the priesthood, too, and sacrificial worship (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.14-Jer.33.18">Jer 33:14-18</reference>); He promises also the everlasting duration of these two ordinances of grace (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.19-Jer.33.22">Jer 33:19-22</reference>), because His covenant with the seed of Jacob and David shall be as enduring as the natural ordinance of day and night, and the laws of heaven and earth (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.23-Jer.33.26">Jer 33:23-26</reference>). - The promises thus fall into two parts. First, there is proclaimed the restoration of the people and kingdom to a new and glorious state of prosperity (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.4-Jer.33.13">Jer 33:4-13</reference>); then the re-establishment of the monarchy and the priesthood to a new and permanent condition (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.14-Jer.33.26">Jer 33:14-26</reference>). In the first part, the promise given in <reference osisRef="Jer.32.36-Jer.32.44">Jer 32:36-44</reference> is further carried out; in the second, the future form of the kingdom is more plainly depicted.
entries.60057f5cc07ec138ac1ea53e992967387b5b3e61: <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2-Jer.33.3">Jer 33:2-3</reference> <hi type="italic">Introduction. -</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference> <hi type="italic">. "Thus saith Jahveh who makes it, Jahveh who forms it in order to establish it, Jahveh is His name:</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference> <hi type="italic">. Call on me and I will answer thee, and tell thee great and hidden things which thou knowest not."</hi> The reference of the suffixes in עשׂהּ, אותהּ, and הכינהּ is evident from the contents of the propositions: the Lord does what He says, and forms what He wants to make, in order to accomplish it, i.e., He completes what He has spoken and determined on. יצר, <hi type="italic">to frame</hi>, namely, in the mind, as if to think out, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jer 18:11</reference> : the expression is parallel with חשׁב; in this sense also we find Isa 46:11. הכין, to establish, realize what has been determined on, prepare, is also found in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference>, but more frequently in Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.12">Jer 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.12">Jer 51:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15">Jer 51:15</reference>), and pretty often in the Old Testament generally. On the phrase "Jahveh is His name," cf. Jer 31:35. The idea contained in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference> reminds us of similar expressions of Isaiah, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Isa 46:11</reference>, etc.; but this similarity offers no foundation for the doubts of Movers and Hitzig regarding the genuineness of this verse. The same holds as regards Jer 33:3. The first proposition occurs frequently in the Psalms, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.4.4">Jer 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jer 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer 30:9</reference>, also in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.27">Jer 7:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">Jer 11:14</reference>; but קתא with אל is unusual in Isaiah. The words בּצרות לא  are certainly an imitation of נצרות ולא ידעתּם, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.6">Isa 48:6</reference>; but they are modified, in the manner peculiar to Jeremiah, by the change of נצרות into בצרות. The combination גּדלות וּבצרות noit is elsewhere used only of the strong cities of the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deu 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.1">Deu 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.14.12">Jos 14:12</reference>, cf. Num 13:28; here בּצרות is transferred to things which lie beyond the limits of human power to discover, and become known to men only through divine revelation. There is no good reason for Ewald’s change of בצרות in accordance with Isa 48:6. - On the contents of these verses Hengstenberg remarks: "It may seem strange that, though in the opening part the prophet is promised a revelation of greater, unknown things, for which he is to call on God, yet the succeeding announcement contains scarcely anything remarkable or peculiar." Graf also adds the remark of Hitzig, that the command to pray, addressed to Jeremiah, cannot have the effect of keeping us from the conclusion that the verses are an addition by a later hand. Nägelsbach replies that the mode of expression presents nothing specially unlike Jeremiah, and that what is most calculated to give the impression of being unlike Jeremiah’s, namely, this introduction in itself, and especially the peculiar turn of <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference>, "Call unto me," etc., is occasioned by the prayer of the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.16">Jer 32:16</reference>-25. To this prayer the prophet had received an answer, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.36-Jer.32.44">Jer 32:36-44</reference>; but he is here admonished to approach the Lord more frequently with such a request. The God who has the power to execute as well as make decrees is quite prepared to give him an insight into His great thoughts regarding the future; and of this a proof is at once given. Thus, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1-Jer.33.3">Jer 33:1-3</reference> must be viewed as the connecting link between Jer 32; 33. <div eID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> Yet these remarks are not sufficient to silence the objections set forth against the genuineness of <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference>; for the specializing title of our chapter, in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1">Jer 33:1</reference>, is opposed to the close connection which Nägelsbach maintains between Jer 32; 33. The fact that, in Jer 32, Jeremiah addresses the Lord in prayer for further revelation regarding the purchase of the field, as commanded, and that he receives the information he desired regarding it, gives no occasion for warning to the prophet, to betake himself more frequently to God for disclosures regarding His purposes of salvation. And Nägelsbach has quite evaded the objection that Jeremiah does not obey the injunction. Moreover, the succeeding revelation made in vv. 4-26 is not of the nature of a "proof," for it does not contain a single great leading feature in God’s purposes as regards the future. - Hengstenberg also points out the difficulty, "that the Scripture everywhere refuses to recognise a dead knowledge as true knowledge, and that the hope of restoration has an obstacle in the natural man, who strives to obscure and to extinguish it; that, consequently, the promise of restoration is always new, and the word of God always great and grand;" but what he adduces for the solution of the difficulty contained in the command, "Call on me, and I will show thee great and unknown things," is insufficient for his purpose. The objection which expositors have taken to these verses has arisen from an improper application of them; the words קרא אלי have been understood as referring to the request that God should give some revelation regarding the future, or His purposes of deliverance, and ענה as referring to the communication of His purposes for increasing our knowledge of them. But "to call on God" rather signifies to pray to God, i.e., to beseech Him for protection, or help, or deliverance in time of need, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Psa 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17">Psa 55:17</reference>, etc.; and to "answer" is the reply of God made when He actually vouchsafes the aid sought for; cf. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.55.17">Psa 55:17</reference>, "I call on God, and Jahveh answers me (saves me);" <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.7">Psa 18:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.7">Psa 27:7</reference>, etc. Consequently, also, "to make known" (הגּיד) is no mere communication of knowledge regarding great and unknown things, no mere letting them be known, but a making known by deeds. The words עשׂהּ and יוצר אותהּ, ascribed to the Lord, suggest and require that the words should be thus understood. With the incorrect reference of these words to knowing and making known there is connected the further error, that the command, "Call unto me," is directed to the person of the prophet, and gives an admonition for his behaviour towards God, for which the text affords on foundation whatever; for it does not run: "Thus saith Jahveh to me" (אלי), and the insertion of this אלי is unwarranted, and inconsistent with the use of כּי which introduces the announcement. Hitzig, Graf, and others have passed by this כּי without remark; and what Nägelsbach says about it is connected with his view, already refuted, as to the essential unity of Jer 32; 33. Lastly, Ewald has enclosed <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference> within parentheses, and considers that the introductory formula of <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference> is resumed in <reference osisRef="Jer.33.4">Jer 33:4</reference> : "Yea, thus saith Jahveh." This is a conclusion hastily formed by one who is in difficulty, for <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference> has not the nature of a parenthesis. If we allow the arbitrary addition "to me" after the words, "Thus saith the Lord," <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference>, and if we take the words in their simplest sense - the invocation of the Lord as a call to God for help in need - then <reference osisRef="Jer.33.2">Jer 33:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference> do not contain a mere prelude to the revelation which follows, but an exhortation to the people to betake themselves to the Lord their God in their calamity, when He will make known to them things unattainable by human discernment; for (כּי, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.4">Jer 33:4</reference>) He announces, in reference to the ruined houses of the city, that He will repair their injuries.
entries.5db54c47f50cae24ec18c220f44dc2f96fa5420d: <reference osisRef="Jer.33.4-Jer.33.6">Jer 33:4-6</reference> <hi type="italic">Repair of the injuries and renewal of the prosperity of Jerusalem and Judah. -
